question: Does God need blood to forgive?
subtitle: And what actually saves?
aliases: why did Jesus have to die
did Jesus die for my sins
without shedding of blood there is no forgiveness
finding: God does not need blood, and Jesus never taught that he did. Every time Jesus is asked directly how a person is saved, he answers with repentance, mercy, commandment-keeping, and forgiving others. Never with his own death. Penal substitution is a Levitical framework laid over a Roman execution: argued by Paul, formalized later, and read back into the gospels by redactors whose hand we can still see in the manuscripts. The prophets had already said it: God desires mercy, not sacrifice. The earliest Christian communion prayers have no blood theology in them at all. We are not minimizing the cross. We are asking who put the price tag on it.
oneLiners: Jesus was asked how to be saved. He answered. It wasn't "believe I'm about to die."
"Forgive and you will be forgiven" and "without blood there is no forgiveness" cannot both be the mechanism.
One gospel out of four adds "for the remission of sins", and it's the one copying from the gospel that doesn't.
He said "I desire mercy, not sacrifice." Twice, both times to the men running the sacrifices.
doNotSay: "Hosea 6:6 is not a comparison." The second line uses comparative min, "more than burnt offerings." Anyone with a Hebrew Bible open will correct you, and the defensible claim is stronger anyway: Jesus deploys the verse twice to overrule the men running the cult.
"The Didache has no sacrifice." Chapter 14 uses the word three times, of the assembly's own offering. Say the prayers of chapters 9–10 have no body, blood or death language.
"Hebrews is anonymous, so discount it." So are all four gospels. Don't hand them a criterion that cuts our own case.
"Jeremiah 7 is the one chapter where God denies ever asking for sacrifice." Say instead: 7:22-23 says the covenant coming out of Egypt wasn't founded on sacrifice but on "obey my voice."

sources.note: Asked point-blank how to inherit eternal life, Jesus names the commandments. Also in Mark 10:19 and Luke 18:20, so not single-source. Know verses 21–31 before you quote 17: the next answer is harder, still an instruction to act, and Peter is promised a hundredfold for doing it.

sources.phrase: if ye forgive men their trespasses
sources.note: Forgiveness is reciprocal and ongoing, not a finished purchase. Also Mark 11:25 and Luke 11:4. The Unforgiving Servant (Matthew 18:21-35) has the king revoke forgiveness already granted; a finished transaction cannot be revoked.

sources.phrase: I will have mercy, and not sacrifice
sources.note: Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6 twice, both times as a rebuke to the men running the cult. He is not reforming sacrifice; he is overruling them.

The verse he is quoting, with its second line. Say the Hebrew carefully: 6:6a is a flat "not"; 6:6b is "more than". Prophetic idiom that subordinates cult to mercy, in the company of Jeremiah 7:22-23, Isaiah 1:11-17, Amos 5:21-25, Psalm 51:16-17 and Micah 6:6-8.

Mark's cup saying has no atonement clause. Matthew 26:28 adds "for the remission of sins" to his Markan source; Luke 22:20, 1 Corinthians 11:25 and the Didache lack it too. Strip the addition and what remains echoes Exodus 24:8: Sinai blood seals a covenant, it does not pay for sins.

sources.title: Didache 9–10
sources.edition: Richardson (1953); Roberts-Donaldson 1886 is public domain and equivalent
sources.note: The oldest Christian communion prayers thank God for what Jesus revealed, "life and knowledge", not for what he paid. Chapters 9–10 contain no body, blood or death. Chapter 14 does use "sacrifice", of the assembly's own offering; say it that precisely.

Jesus's brother, head of the Jerusalem church, states it plainly. "Faith alone" occurs once in the New Testament, here, as the thing being denied. Same verb as Romans 4:2, same patriarch, opposite verdicts.

Expect this first. It is the strongest verse against us and it has no redaction escape hatch. Concede the text. Then: lytron is a release-payment to a captor, not sacrificial vocabulary; Leviticus never uses it for sin offerings. And the paragraph (10:42-45) is about status, not atonement: "whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister."

"Jesus himself said his blood was shed for the forgiveness of sins." In exactly one source: Matthew, editing Mark toward his own program (compare 1:21, also his addition). Direction of editing, not source-counting, is the criterion, and the card runs it on our own texts too.

sources.tier: early church · not Jesus, not Paul
sources.phrase: without shedding of blood is no remission
sources.note: A first-century theologian's reading of Leviticus applied to the crucifixion after the fact, which is exactly what is in dispute. Set it beside Jesus quoting Hosea 6:6 twice and choose which stack you build on. Don't argue "it's anonymous": so are the gospels.

The known counterpunch to Jeremiah 7:22. Concede it without hedging. Then: 7:22-23 is about what the covenant was founded on ("obey my voice"); 33:14-26 is absent from the Septuagint Jeremiah entirely; and the prophetic case survives both.

Isaiah 53 in Jesus's own mouth. Concede it, then look at which clause he quotes: "reckoned among the transgressors", about his arrest, not a payment mechanism. Luke 24:47 names the outcome: repentance and remission proclaimed. Luke drops Mark's ransom clause at 22:27.

sources.phrase: by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified
sources.note: "Nobody can keep the commandments, which is the whole point." That argument is Paul's, not Jesus's. Jesus says "my yoke is easy" (Matthew 11:30) and "this do, and thou shalt live" (Luke 10:28). Paul answers a different question: what Paul taught.

sources.title: Anselm, Cur Deus Homo, Book I
sources.note: Satisfaction theory: sin is a debt to God's honor that only a God-man can pay. The courtroom logic most churches teach today is this book's, not the gospels'. Calvin (Institutes II.16, 1536) turns satisfaction into penal substitution.

sources.phrase: whosoever doth not bear his cross, and come after me
sources.note: Q's one cross saying is about the follower's cross. The double tradition has no sentence calling his death a sacrifice, a ransom or a payment. That doesn't mean the compilers denied the crucifixion; they didn't build on it.
